title.en: Analytic derivative against a finite difference with step study

summary: Cross-check an analytic directional derivative with a central difference and expose the step size where cancellation takes over.
objective: Analytic and numerical values agree within declared absolute and relative bounds for the declared fixture, and the zero-gradient point draws no steepest direction.
applies_when: A scene displays a derivative, slope or gradient computed analytically.
A viewer can choose a direction or a probe point continuously.
The domain contains a critical point where the gradient vanishes.
intent_signals: what happens at the flat point of the surface
example_prompts: Cross-check the directional derivative readout on this surface.

principles: An analytic derivative and a finite difference are two independent computations; agreement to a stated order is evidence, and the pattern of disagreement identifies which one is wrong.

A step-size optimum exists only when truncation error is present: the central difference is exact for a quadratic in exact arithmetic, so on the common quadratic fixture only cancellation grows as the step shrinks. Demonstrating the order needs a fixture with a nonzero third derivative, and the fixture is declared with the expectation.

The zero-gradient point is its own regime: no direction is steepest there and the directional derivative is zero in every direction, so probe directions there are arbitrary declared unit vectors rather than a gradient direction that does not exist.
implementation: State the function, its smoothness and the coordinate scale, then at each probe evaluate the analytic directional derivative as the gradient dotted with a unit direction and, independently, a central difference along the same direction with both offset points inside the domain.

Repeat over step sizes spanning several orders of magnitude on both fixtures, the quadratic and one with a nonzero third derivative, and record the error at each so the actual curve shape is observed rather than assumed.

At probes with a nonzero gradient include three characteristic directions: along the gradient, opposite to it and perpendicular to it. At a zero-gradient probe use two arbitrary declared unit directions instead.
Probe the zero-gradient point explicitly and record what the interface displays for a steepest direction there.
observable_checks: Central-difference and analytic values agree within a combined absolute and relative bound stated from the function and coordinate scales, since relative error is undefined where the derivative is zero. On the nonzero-third-derivative fixture the error falls roughly with the square of the step until cancellation dominates and that turning point is reported; on the quadratic fixture no truncation branch appears, which is the expected result rather than a failure.
Opposite directions give equal magnitudes with opposite signs, and a direction perpendicular to a nonzero gradient gives zero within the declared absolute bound rather than a relative one.
At the zero-gradient point both declared probe directions return zero within the absolute bound and no steepest-direction arrow is drawn; drawing an arbitrary arrow there is the failure signal.

known_limits: Cross-checks the derivative of a declared analytic function; it does not validate a triangulated surface as a model of that function.
Authored verification guidance; no computation or render was run for this record.
creative_affordances: Adapt the scenario, scale and presentation to your subject; this record fixes what must be checked, not how the scene must look.

claims.statement: The directional derivative of a differentiable function along a unit vector equals the gradient dotted with that vector, and when the gradient is zero the directional derivative is zero for every unit vector.
claims.scope: Differentiable scalar functions with a unit domain direction, as stated in the cited theorem and gradient properties.

source_refs.locator: 4.6, Theorem 4.12 and the gradient properties that follow

claims.statement: Catastrophic cancellation occurs when nearby quantities carrying rounding error are subtracted, so accurate digits of the difference disappear.
claims.scope: Binary floating-point arithmetic as described in the cited section; the size of the effect depends on the expression and the precision used.
